title: Claim Denials and Appeals

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe claim denials and distinguish them from claim rejections.
- Explain the claim appeal process, including its levels, documentation, and deadlines.
- Distinguish corrections from appeals and apply the correct resolution for common denial scenarios.
- Explain the documentation and timely-response requirements that support effective denial resolution and appeals.
- Apply scope-of-practice boundaries by escalating clinical, coding, and coverage decisions to appropriate staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A denial is like a store telling you, after looking at your receipt, 'we are not going to give you a refund.' It is a final 'no' that you can ask them to think about again.

### Question 2

A rejection is like mailing a letter with a wrong address; it comes right back before anyone reads it, so you fix the address and send it again.

### Question 3

A rejection is a package sent back before it is opened; a denial is a package that was opened and answered 'no.' Each one needs a different fix.

### Question 4

Checking your facts before you send something — like making sure a package address is right before mailing — stops most problems before they happen.

### Question 5

A remittance advice is like a store receipt that shows what they paid you, what they did not, and the reason written next to each item.

### Question 6

The EOB is the note the insurance company sends to the patient, like a receipt that says what they paid and what the patient might still owe.

### Question 7

A reason code is like a short answer key that tells you why the insurance company paid less or paid nothing at all.

### Question 8

CO is like a store's 'final sale' sign — the provider agreed ahead of time to accept this, so the patient does not have to pay it.

### Question 9

PR is like the part of a restaurant bill that is your share to pay, like your half of a shared meal.

### Question 10

If you wrote the wrong date on a form, you would just fix the date and hand it back — you would not argue about it. A corrected claim is the 'fix the date' move.

### Question 11

An appeal is like asking a teacher to re-grade a test because you think a correct answer was marked wrong.

### Question 12

A duplicate denial is like being told 'you already turned in this homework' — the same paper was handed in twice.

### Question 13

A timely filing denial is like turning in homework after the teacher already closed the gradebook — it was too late to be accepted.

### Question 14

Checking that a coupon is still valid before you try to use it saves you from a surprise at the register.

### Question 15

A write-off is like erasing a number from someone's bill because the store agreed not to charge it or knows it will not be paid.

### Question 16

If you forgot to write a required label on a form, you would add the label and send it again — not argue about it.

### Question 17

An appeal is for when you disagree with a decision and want to show your evidence — like showing the teacher your correct work to change a grade.

### Question 18

Before you fix anything, you read the note that says what went wrong — otherwise you might fix the wrong thing.

### Question 19

An appeal has steps, like climbing a ladder — you start on the first rung (redetermination) before you can reach the higher ones.

### Question 20

If you miss the deadline to ask for a re-check, you may not get another chance — just like missing the last day to turn in a contest entry.

### Question 21

To prove a service was needed, you show the evidence — the notes and test results — just like showing your work to prove an answer.

### Question 22

A letter of medical necessity is like a note from your doctor explaining exactly why you need a certain treatment so the insurance company understands.

### Question 23

Fixing a typo is a correction; asking someone to change their mind is an appeal. They are two different tools for two different jobs.

### Question 24

A corrected claim needs a special sticker saying 'this is a corrected version' so the office does not think you sent the same paper twice.

### Question 25

A timely filing limit is like a homework due date — if you turn it in late, the teacher (payer) may not accept it.

### Question 26

If the store made a mistake on your refund, you would show the receipt and ask them to look again — politely and with proof.

### Question 27

A 'not covered' denial means the service is not on the list of things the plan will pay for — like ordering something not on the menu.

### Question 28

A denial log is like a checklist of everything that went wrong, so you can fix each item and stop the same mistakes from happening again.

### Question 29

If someone asks for the proof you forgot to include, you send the proof — you do not start an argument.

### Question 30

A deductible is like the first part of a bill you agreed to pay yourself before the plan starts helping.

### Question 31

If the first checker says no, you can ask a different, independent checker to look at it — that is the reconsideration step.

### Question 32

Keeping copies is like saving your proof of mailing and every reply, so you can show exactly what you sent and when.

### Question 33

Only the person who wrote the notes may add a correction, and they must mark it clearly — you never change someone else's notes yourself.

### Question 34

Fixing a record is like adding a dated note that says 'I want to add this now' — you keep the old writing and add the new part on top.

### Question 35

You cannot change an answer on the form just to get a 'yes' — the codes must honestly match what the doctor wrote down.

### Question 36

You can tell someone you sent the request and will let them know the answer, but you cannot promise what the answer will be.

### Question 37

A peer-to-peer review is like two doctors talking it over so the insurance company's doctor can understand why the treatment was needed.

### Question 38

The assistant is the helper who gathers the papers and keeps track of dates, while the doctors and billing experts make the big decisions.

### Question 39

Prevention is checking everything before you start, so you do not have to fix problems later.

### Question 40

Root cause analysis is like figuring out why the leak keeps happening and fixing the pipe, instead of just mopping the floor every time.

### Question 41

When two insurance plans are involved, you have to figure out which one goes first, like deciding which parent signs the permission slip first.

### Question 42

A reopening is like asking someone to fix a small typo on your bill right away, instead of starting a whole formal complaint.

### Question 43

When you have truly tried everything, you close the account the right way and write down what happened, instead of pretending it never happened.

### Question 44

These codes are like labels on a receipt that tell you who pays each part: you, the office, or someone else.

### Question 45

A clean claim is like a homework paper that is complete and neat, so the teacher can grade it without asking for missing pages.

### Question 46

External review is like asking a neutral referee, who is not on either team, to look at the decision one more time.

### Question 47

An ABN is like warning someone before they order that the meal might not be on the plan, so they can decide if they still want it and will pay.

### Question 48

You can ask someone to pay for something only if you warned them beforehand and they agreed — you cannot surprise them with a bill afterward.

### Question 49

A good appeal is like a well-organized argument: say who you are, what you want, and show your evidence.

### Question 50

Including the original number is like writing 'revision of form #7' so everyone knows this new paper replaces the old one.

### Question 51

This code says 'we do not think this was needed,' so you respond by showing the evidence that it was needed.

### Question 52

If you are told you turned something in late, you check your records and show the receipt proving you were on time.

### Question 53

A clearinghouse is like a proofreader that checks your paper for mistakes before you hand it in.

### Question 54

Before you buy something that needs permission, you get the permission first so there is no surprise 'no' later.

### Question 55

Fixing a code is a job for the trained expert, like having the right specialist repair something instead of guessing.

### Question 56

There are two separate due dates: one for turning in the paper and another for asking for a re-check after it is graded.

### Question 57

After you send a request, you keep an eye on it and answer quickly if someone asks for more information, instead of forgetting about it.

### Question 58

A contractual adjustment is the agreed discount the office accepts; a denial is a 'no' on the whole item.

### Question 59

When you are not sure what to do, you ask the person who knows, instead of guessing.

### Question 60

Work on the oldest items first, like doing the homework that is due soonest, so nothing gets forgotten.

### Question 61

If the store paid you only part of what they owe, you show them the price tag and ask for the rest — you do not just give up.

### Question 62

Balance billing is trying to charge the customer extra on top of the agreed price, which the contract says you are not allowed to do.

### Question 63

Some services are counted as part of a bigger service, so you only add a special 'these were separate' marker when that is really true.

### Question 64

An administrative denial is about paperwork mistakes; a clinical denial is about whether the treatment was really needed.

### Question 65

If you send a form and hear nothing back, you do not assume anything — you check in and ask what happened to it.

### Question 66

Share only the pages you need, not the whole notebook — just enough to prove your point while keeping the rest private.

### Question 67

A modifier is a note that says 'these two were really separate,' and you only add it when the notes prove it.

### Question 68

A query is like politely asking the doctor to explain their notes more clearly so the paperwork matches what really happened.

### Question 69

Writing down when and how you sent something is like saving your 'sent' timestamp so you can prove you mailed it on time.

### Question 70

If you lose round one, you can decide to go to round two — but only if you act before the next deadline.

### Question 71

When a customer is confused about a bill, you explain it kindly and get help from an expert if the question is too hard.

### Question 72

This denial says the plan thinks the treatment is still 'being tested' and will not pay, so you may need to show proof it works.

### Question 73

One 'no' happens before you do the work and the other after — like being told no before or after you already bought something.

### Question 74

The second insurance company needs to see the first one's receipt before it pays its share, so you attach that receipt.

### Question 75

An appeal is a formal 'please look again' with your proof, and you have to send it by the due date.

### Question 76

For Medicare's first appeal, you usually have about four months (120 days) to ask them to look again.

### Question 77

If someone asks for more proof by a certain day, you send it on time and keep a copy, or you might lose the whole request.

### Question 78

A date and signature on a note are like the name and date on a test — they show who wrote it and when, so it can be trusted.

### Question 79

Writing down every mistake and sorting them by type shows you which mistakes keep happening, so you can stop them.

### Question 80

Retroactive authorization is asking for permission after the fact, and sometimes the answer can still be yes — but you have to ask.

### Question 81

If you had permission all along but forgot to write the permission number, adding that number fixes the whole thing.

### Question 82

This means the payer thinks the second service was already part of the first one it paid for, so you only push back if the notes show they were truly separate.

### Question 83

Good notes are the evidence that proves your case — without them, there is nothing to show the insurance company.

### Question 84

If you notice a repeated mistake, you tell the person in charge so it can be fixed — you do not cover it up.

### Question 85

A remark code is like the extra sentence the insurance company writes under the short code, explaining in more words why it changed or refused something.

### Question 86

This is a 'check the ID badge' problem — you verify the doctor's status with the insurance company instead of guessing.

### Question 87

Denials are like expiring coupons — if you wait too long to use them, they become worthless.

### Question 88

A corrected claim is for fixing mistakes on the form; an appeal is for arguing about the decision.

### Question 89

Only the doctor can say a treatment was really needed; the assistant passes that question to the doctor instead of answering for them.

### Question 90

The goal is to figure out what went wrong, fix it the right way before time runs out, and stop it from happening again.
